brief.text: Pakistan’s civil so­ci­ety is dis­tinct from what Pranay Kotasthane calls its mil­i­tary-jihadi com­plex, Amit Varma said. That state draws le­git­i­macy from paint­ing India as the enemy, and op­presses its peo­ple. {122-C02}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma argues that nationalism harms every nation
lead.head: Love the country, not the ism

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma in Episode 122

body: The day after India beat Pakistan at cricket, Amit Varma scrolled through Twitter and was deeply dis­turbed. The play­ers had re­fused to shake hands. The cap­tain and politi­cians had made bel­liger­ent noises, and so­cial media had erupted after the win.
It made no sense to him. Indian and Pakistani crick­eters have al­ways been friendly, he said, and Pakistani com­men­ta­tors such as Wasim Akram are “su­perbly pop­u­lar among our peo­ple”.

For the com­mon per­son, Varma ar­gued, na­tion­al­ism means doing what Doug Stanhope once de­scribed: “hat­ing peo­ple you have never met and tak­ing pride in ac­com­plish­ments you had noth­ing to do with”. {122-S01}

He began by pulling apart three ideas that are often con­fused. The na­tional in­ter­est, he said, is what is good for your coun­try; pa­tri­o­tism is love for your coun­try. Nationalism is “an ide­ol­ogy that I largely tend to think of as kind of toxic”. {122-C01}
His the­sis fol­lowed: “Nationalism is bad for the na­tion. Any na­tion­al­ism, any na­tion.”
## Strangers in one imag­ined fam­ily

The def­i­ni­tion Varma likes best is Benedict Anderson’s: a na­tion is an imag­ined po­lit­i­cal com­mu­nity. Unlike a small tribe, it is made mostly of peo­ple we will never meet. “We don’t even know their pref­er­ences by and large,” Varma said, “but we imag­ine it to be some­thing which we de­fine nar­rowly.” {122-C04}

The tribal in­stinct be­neath it is an­cient; the na­tion is new. Nations are only a few cen­turies old, yet each claims a glo­ri­ous past, which has to be in­vented. The scholar Shruti Kapila, Varma re­called, once called Hindutva “a the­ory of vi­o­lence in search of a his­tory”.
In Europe, he said, the print­ing press, re­vived ver­nac­u­lars and the Romantic move­ment made na­tions pos­si­ble. Social media, Varma sus­pects, is today’s print­ing press.
## Every good has a twin

Varma granted that na­tion­al­ism can unite the colonised, bind com­mu­ni­ties and re­vive cul­tures. But every good, he ar­gued, has a match­ing harm, and the goods can be had in other ways. “You don’t ac­tu­ally need to in­vent a shared iden­tity to do it.” {122-C09}

His deep­est ob­jec­tion is that na­tion­al­ism, like other iden­tity ide­olo­gies, es­sen­tialises. “You are tying me down to an iden­tity of birth or lo­ca­tion, and you are telling me this is who you are,” he said. That, he ar­gued, de­hu­man­ises. {122-C11}

Ajay Shah added that na­tion­al­ism helps the state, the people’s hired agent, be­come their ruler. Once you blur the peo­ple of Italy and the Italian gov­ern­ment, he said, the gov­ern­ment “lays claim to the idea that they rep­re­sent Italy”.
Mussolini, Hitler and Putin, Shah noted, all ended by pour­ing their own peo­ple into war.
## Closer to home

In India, Varma counted three na­tion­alisms born under the British: Hindutva, a Muslim na­tion­al­ism that be­came Pakistan, and the sec­u­lar na­tion­al­ism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. All, he said, are imag­ined.
The sec­u­lar idea won, but it was im­posed from the top. “People like us failed be­cause we could not do it from the bot­tom up.”
Nationalism also in­vades ev­ery­day life, Varma ar­gued: lan­guage, sport, music, clothes and food. Behind eco­nomic na­tion­al­ism, Shah said, “what’s re­ally going on is just pro­tec­tion­ism”.
Varma closed with a plea. Nationalism, he said, di­min­ishes us eco­nom­i­cally, cul­tur­ally and in char­ac­ter. “So na­tion­al­ism is a great di­min­ish­ment of the self.”
Shah re­called a wish he at­trib­uted to Rabindranath Tagore: “the winds from the seven con­ti­nents to blow through my na­tion”.

second.label: India and Pakistan
second.head: A mother’s gold medal
second.deck: Amit Varma’s antidote to cricket’s bad blood came from a javelin thrower’s home

pic.caption: Neeraj Chopra at Bauhaus-Galan in Stockholm in 2022

body: When Neeraj Chopra won the javelin gold two Olympics ago, Amit Varma re­called, one of the peo­ple he praised was Pakistan’s Arshad Nadeem, a close friend whom Neeraj had al­ways en­cour­aged, al­most like a men­tor.

At the last Olympics it was Arshad who won gold, with what Varma called an out­lier throw of “ninety two point some­thing”, and a dis­ap­pointed Neeraj did not. A TV crew went to Neeraj’s mother to ask how she felt. {#mother} Arshad, she said, was her son too.
That, Varma said, is the sen­ti­ment you want be­tween Indians and Pakistanis. “Frankly, we are the same damn peo­ple here. It’s the same damn cul­ture.” {122-S07}

quote.text: Because a state will al­ways in­voke na­tion­al­ism to strengthen its own pow­ers and to turn us against each other.

third.head: Full marks for Shudh Hindi

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on acing Hindi with Shudh words, with Ajay Shah

body: In both the 10th and 12th stan­dard, Amit Varma scored more marks in Hindi than in English. He was lazy, he ad­mit­ted in stronger words, and did not re­ally study. But he had hacked Hindi.

The hack was to learn lots of Shudh Hindi words, dwar in­stead of dar­waza, mitra in­stead of dost, and string them to­gether. Teachers re­warded it, he said, “be­cause no­body speaks in Shudh Hindi”. {122-S06}

Schoolroom Hindi, Varma ar­gued, was con­structed. The north’s liv­ing lan­guage grew bot­tom up as a khichdi of in­flu­ences; then Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was con­sciously pro­moted. {122-C15}
Imagine English speak­ers using only Latinate words, he said. Instead of “we shall fight them in the streets”, Winston Churchill would have said “we shall com­bat them in the boule­vards”. {122-J03}

p2.title: Nationalism on trial
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s case that nationalism is bad for the nation, chapter by chapter, with Ajay Shah’s interjections

from1.head: Love the country, not the ism

quote.text: Nationalism is not the awak­en­ing of na­tions to self con­scious­ness. It in­vents na­tions where they do not exist.
quote.who: Ernest Gellner, as quoted by Amit Varma

photo.caption: Benedict Anderson at University College Dublin in 2012

box.title: A book to begin with
box.text: Benedict Anderson’s *Imagined Communities* is pos­si­bly Amit Varma’s favourite book on na­tion­al­ism. It gave the episode its def­i­ni­tion of a na­tion, an imag­ined po­lit­i­cal com­mu­nity, lim­ited and sov­er­eign, and its three para­doxes of na­tion­hood. {122-R01}

sections.label: What it is
sections.head: Nobody has met the nation
sections.caption: the imagined community
body: Every na­tion is imag­ined, Amit Varma ar­gued. His def­i­ni­tion comes from Benedict Anderson’s *Imagined Communities*: a na­tion is an imag­ined po­lit­i­cal com­mu­nity. {122-R01}

The in­stincts be­neath it are an­cient. Humans evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes, where sol­i­dar­ity with your own and sus­pi­cion of the other were se­lected for. “And we evolved in those times to be trib­al­is­tic.” {122-C03}

The philoso­pher W. E. H. Lecky de­scribed a cir­cle of moral con­cern that ex­pands over time, from kin to tribe to vil­lage. Peter Singer pre­dicted it would one day take in an­i­mals. “Alas,” Varma said, “it hasn’t even ex­panded to in­clude all human be­ings.”
The na­tion is one stage of that cir­cle. Unlike a band of Dunbar’s 150, its mem­bers are mostly strangers, yet we imag­ine them as one ho­mo­ge­neous peo­ple. {122-C04}
## Three para­doxes

Anderson found three para­doxes in it. Nations are a few cen­turies old, yet each claims a glo­ri­ous past. {122-C05} Everyone sup­pos­edly has a na­tion­al­ity, yet each is unique. And na­tion­al­ism is a def­i­nite po­lit­i­cal force that is philo­soph­i­cally neb­u­lous.

There are no great thinkers of na­tion­al­ism, Varma said. Ajay Shah ob­jected that Mussolini had the­ory; we are just loath to ac­cept it. Varma replied that Mussolini, Hitler and Savarkar of­fered as­ser­tions, not first prin­ci­ples. “To me you don’t qual­ify as a se­ri­ous thinker un­less you can tell me the why.” {122-C06}
~ Such men, he said, are men of ac­tion, and their world­view is a ra­tio­nal­i­sa­tion for the ter­ri­ble things they do.

quote.text: Nationalism is not the awak­en­ing of na­tions to self con­scious­ness. It in­vents na­tions where they do not exist.
quote.who: Ernest Gellner, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: How it spread
sections.head: Roses, presses and Pushkin
sections.caption: how nationalism spread
body: In the Europe of the 1300s and 1400s there were no na­tions, Amit Varma said, only king­doms, em­pires and local loy­al­ties, in days be­fore maps or the print­ing press.

Some his­to­ri­ans date English con­scious­ness to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses. The dy­nas­tic civil war swept away many feu­dal over­lords, and with them the local al­le­giance owed to them. Commoners and roy­als fought side by side and began to feel part of the same peo­ple. {122-S02}
Varma dead­panned that *The War of the Roses* was a 1989 film, re­cently re­made as *The Roses*, “but that is com­pletely dif­fer­ent”. {122-J02}
## Presses and folk songs

Revived ver­nac­u­lars such as French and German gave peo­ple a com­mon marker, and the print­ing press gave their sto­ries scale. {#printing} Locke and Rousseau’s will of the peo­ple needed a peo­ple. The Romantic move­ment, re­act­ing against a coldly ra­tio­nal Enlightenment, sup­plied the folk songs and fairy tales.

Russia shows how sticky the thread is. The Tsars used Russification; the com­mu­nists railed against na­tion­al­ism; yet at a 1937 cel­e­bra­tion of the Soviet Union’s great poets, in Stalin’s time, the Russian Pushkin was feted above all. {122-S04}
~ By the end of the 19th cen­tury, he said, na­tion­al­ism ruled the world. {#rules}

quote.text: One of my the­o­ries for the re­vival and ex­ac­er­ba­tion of mod­ern na­tion­al­ism is that so­cial media en­ables that kind of prim­i­tive trib­al­ism

sections.label: Good and bad
sections.head: Every ‘we’ needs a ‘them’
sections.caption: the yin and yang of nationalism
body: Amit Varma gave na­tion­al­ism its due, then showed the flip side of each good. It can unite the colonised against their rulers, but every op­pres­sor uses it too. The German the­o­rist Carl Schmitt said pol­i­tics needs an other, and na­tion­al­ism sup­plies one au­to­mat­i­cally. {122-J19}

It can bind peo­ple to­gether, but the mo­ment you say we are a Hindu na­tion or a Muslim na­tion, some­one else is oth­ered. It can re­vive a cul­ture, but call­ing one tra­di­tion ours de­clares oth­ers not ours.
The goods, he ar­gued, come from else­where too: self-government, the eco­nomic web of cities, shared tastes such as the cult that fol­lows The Peter Cat Recording Company. {122-R14}
## Love with­out pride
Ajay Shah cringes at the word pride. Varma loves Van Morrison, Shah pointed out, but is not proud of him. “Pride is some­thing you have got to have done some­thing.” {122-C10}

Worst of all, Varma said, na­tion­al­ism ties you to an ac­ci­dent of birth and de­clares it the most im­por­tant thing about you, baaki sab jaaye bhaad mein. That, he ar­gued, de­hu­man­ises: it de­nies the mul­ti­tudes each of us con­tains. {122-C11}

~ Shah added a pub­lic-choice view: the peo­ple are the prin­ci­pal and the state their agent. Nationalism, he said, has played an im­por­tant role in the trick that turns cit­i­zens into sub­jects. {122-C12}

quote.text: I con­tain mul­ti­tudes, as do all of you.

sections.label: Gone wrong
sections.head: The cauldron of war
sections.caption: nationalism gone wrong
body: Benito Mussolini spelt out the trick him­self, Amit Varma said, and read out his words: “It is not the peo­ple who make the state, but the state that makes the peo­ple.” {122-J20}

Mussolini sold Italians the glo­ries of an­cient Rome. Hitler built his na­tion­al­ism on race, oth­er­ing a peo­ple to the point of geno­cide and seek­ing Lebensraum, a Germany ex­pand­ing into other lands.
Both coun­tries learnt from their mis­takes, Varma said. Much of the rest of the world is in­tent on re­peat­ing them.
## Same game, dif­fer­ent flag

Communism, with its class war, might seem nationalism’s op­po­site. But both build an in-group and paint ev­ery­one else as the enemy, and Varma traced the Tsars’ Russification through Stalin’s Russia to Putin’s.
For a mo­ment, a bet­ter world seemed near: Francis Fukuyama spoke of the end of his­tory, “though you will note with the ques­tion mark at the end of the orig­i­nal essay”. {122-R08}
Now even the United States has turned to eco­nomic na­tion­al­ism. It is, Varma said, “like we’re in a bad video game sim­u­la­tion and there’s a bug in the sys­tem”. {122-J12}
~ “If only Vladimir Putin could sign on for Rabindranath Tagore as his spir­i­tual guide in­stead of Alexander Dugin,” Ajay Shah said, “then mil­lions of Russians would be alive today.” {122-J22}

quote.text: What worse de­struc­tion of the peo­ple could you achieve other than build­ing this caul­dron of war and pour­ing your own peo­ple into the war?

sections.label: India’s journey
sections.head: A khichdi, then a cleavage
sections.caption: India’s three nationalisms
body: North India’s lan­guage, Amit Varma said, grew “through spon­ta­neous order in this beau­ti­ful bot­tom up way”, a khichdi of Persian, Sanskrit, Prakrit and tongues now dis­missed as di­alects. {122-C15} A lan­guage, as he put it, is a di­alect with an army. {122-J26}

Then pol­i­tics split it. After 1857, he said, the British tried to di­vide and rule, and move­ments within both re­li­gions pulled apart. Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was con­sciously pro­moted. Yet the two re­main mu­tu­ally in­tel­li­gi­ble.
## Three ideas of India

Under the British, three na­tion­alisms grew: a Hindutva aimed more at Muslims than at the British, a Muslim na­tion­al­ism that be­came Pakistan, and the sec­u­lar na­tion­al­ism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. All three, Varma ar­gued, are imag­ined.

The sec­u­lar one won, but it was im­posed from the top while so­ci­ety, as Akshaya Mukul’s book on the Gita Press shows, held other ideas. Those who shared the sec­u­lar vi­sion, he said, failed be­cause they could not build it from the bot­tom up. {122-C14}
Even Ambedkar, Varma noted, called the con­sti­tu­tion a mere top­soil. {122-J25}

~ Rabindranath Tagore saw the dan­ger a cen­tury ago. He backed Indian in­de­pen­dence, Varma said, yet called na­tion­al­ism “a cruel epi­demic of evil eat­ing into humanity’s moral vi­tal­ity”. {122-J23}

quote.text: The na­tion, with its flags and pious hymns, can­not hide the fact that the na­tion is the great­est evil for the earth.
quote.who: Rabindranath Tagore, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Everyday life
sections.head: Biryani is not anti-national
sections.caption: nationalism in everyday life
body: Nationalism does not stay on maps, Amit Varma said. It in­vades sport, food, music, clothes and money.
In *The Sporting Spirit*, George Orwell de­scribed sport as war minus the shoot­ing. {122-J15}

Varma, a sport lover, backs foot­ball teams for their play­ing phi­los­o­phy rather than any badge. Ajay Shah, who does not watch sport, pro­posed ran­dom teams with “a lit­tle bit of old fash­ioned cap­i­tal­ism” in the buy­ing and sell­ing of play­ers.

Most of what India eats came from out­side, Varma said, so food na­tion­al­ism is ridicu­lous. As for the rhetoric about Ajmal Kasab being fed biryani: “Biryani is not anti na­tional,” he said. “I am never going to give up biryani.” {122-J09}
## Pune or Poland

Every vol­un­tary trade is pos­i­tive-sum, “a dou­ble thank you”, Varma said, whether with Pune or Poland. Shah asked what an Indian com­pany even is: about 90 per cent of ICICI Bank’s share­hold­ing is for­eign, he said, and Infosys has mostly for­eign share­hold­ers and cus­tomers. {#icici}

Keeping data on Indian soil means pay­ing for India’s heat, patchy elec­tric­ity, scarce top-end en­gi­neers and tar­iff-inflated equip­ment. The data cen­tre should sit in Greenland, Shah said, where the air is cold. {#greenland}
~ Most of the time, Shah said, “the firms want to cry mummy and get a gov­ern­ment to sup­port them when they are not able to suc­ceed on their own steam”. {122-C17}

quote.text: Somebody will say data is a new crude oil, which is sup­posed to be a check­mate.
And if we just em­brace that and throw our­selves into that and learn from oth­ers and lis­ten to their music and learn other lan­guages, our lives are much richer.

p3.title: Accidents of history
p3.deck: Four tales Amit Varma told, from a caliphate to a football war

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a promise, an alliance and a man’s bitterness
stories.head: Exit the last great moderate
body: Mohandas Gandhi came back from South Africa around 1914, Amit Varma said, and met his great hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale. {#gandhi1914}
Gokhale found him a bit naive. Do not en­gage in ac­tive pol­i­tics, he told Gandhi; prom­ise me that for a year you will just travel around India. Gandhi agreed. A month later, Gokhale died.
Gandhi kept his prom­ise any­way, and chose, for some rea­son, to travel bare­foot as a trib­ute. “I don’t know what the logic of that is,” Varma said, “but he does that.” {122-J13}
At a Congress gath­er­ing around 1917 or 1918, no­body took him se­ri­ously. He was, in Varma’s words, “this ran­dom weird guy who’s come from South Africa”.

His key mo­ment came when he joined the Ali broth­ers and their Khilafat move­ment, which wanted the caliphate, abol­ished at the end of the First World War, re­vived for the broader Muslim Ummah. Gandhi wanted an in­de­pen­dent India. “There’s no co­her­ent rea­son for them to come to­gether, but they do.” {122-S05}

It proved a tac­ti­cal mas­ter­stroke: around 1920 and 1921, Gandhi took over the Congress. The great mod­er­ates of the past had died out, and the last of them, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, thought he would be the next head of the Congress.

Jinnah could not fig­ure Gandhi out. What, he won­dered, did Khilafat have to do with an in­de­pen­dent India? Embittered, he changed com­pletely, stopped being a mod­er­ate and be­came the big­gest pro­po­nent of Pakistan.
~ “In a sense the rest is his­tory,” Varma said.
stories.why: Borders and na­tion­alisms that look eter­nal can turn on ac­ci­dents: a prom­ise to a men­tor who died a month later, an al­liance of con­ve­nience, one man’s bit­ter­ness. Such ac­ci­dents of his­tory, Varma said, can “lead to crazy con­se­quences”. {#crazy}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Gandhi, Khilafat and Jinnah

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a football rivalry that became a war
stories.head: Qualifying for a war
body: In 1969, Amit Varma said, Honduras and El Salvador played a se­ries of qual­i­fy­ing matches for the foot­ball World Cup. There was so much slo­ga­neer­ing and fight­ing dur­ing them that a war fol­lowed. {122-S08}
As he re­called it, the war lasted 100 days, and six thou­sand peo­ple died. {#soccerwar} It is com­monly called the Soccer War.
“It is not that soc­cer caused the war,” Varma said. “Nationalism caused the war, but soc­cer was the trig­ger.”

~ Varma set it be­side George Orwell’s essay *The Sporting Spirit*, which, if he re­mem­bered cor­rectly, looked at an ugly foot­ball match be­tween Glasgow and Moscow, and be­side Hitler’s use of the 1936 Berlin Olympics to drive his rhetoric. {#berlin}
stories.why: Sport is tribal, but it does not start these fires; it am­pli­fies pas­sions na­tion­al­ism has al­ready stoked. In a sense, Varma said, he is happy Pakistan has no great chess play­ers yet: a Gukesh win over a Pakistani would re­vive the same rhetoric.

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on the Soccer War, with Ajay Shah

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Mussolini sold Italy its lost glory
stories.head: All roads lead to the trenchocracy
body: Benito Mussolini came to power in the early 1920s, Amit Varma said, just after the First World War. He ral­lied the peo­ple by promis­ing that Italy would be ruled by the tren­choc­racy: the com­mon peo­ple who had fought in the war. {#trench}

Mussolini was con­ve­niently lo­cated where the Roman Empire had been. Look at the glo­ri­ous Roman Empire, he told Italians: they were there, we are here, how far we have fallen. {#rome} He spoke of Roman mil­i­tary val­our and dis­ci­pline, and did things with pomp and grandeur.

It worked. All through his dis­as­trous reign, Varma said, Mussolini was supremely pop­u­lar. “He didn’t even need to be au­thor­i­tar­ian in that sense. The peo­ple were with him be­cause this was such a pop­u­lar nar­ra­tive.” {122-S03}
~ We know the dis­as­ters of Italian fas­cism, Varma said, and where it took Europe.
stories.why: A story of lost glory can do the work of co­er­cion. Promise a peo­ple their golden age back, and they may fol­low a strong­man into dis­as­ter of their own free will.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on clothes, religion and how labels change
stories.head: What’s Muslim about a salwar?
body: What Amit Varma wore for the episode could be called a pathani suit, or a kurta with a Patiala sal­war. Is it Muslim or Hindu? “The ques­tion is ridicu­lous,” he said. “Clothes don’t have re­li­gion.” {122-S10}
Yet many peo­ple, he said, would call his dress Muslim: some­thing worn at Eid, or a sign that you are prob­a­bly a Muslim. “Which is ab­so­lutely ter­ri­ble.”

When he was grow­ing up in the 1970s and 1980s, sal­war kameez was frowned upon even for women, seen as some­thing Muslim women wear. A Kashmiri Pandit, once a close friend, told Varma he did not let his sis­ter wear it. Now, Varma said, it is com­pletely nor­malised.
~ He reached for an un­likely au­thor­ity. As Bob Dylan once said, he re­minded lis­ten­ers, even the pres­i­dent of the United States must some­day stand naked. {122-J28}
stories.why: Identity pol­i­tics as­signs clothes a faith, and the la­bels can flip within a gen­er­a­tion, as sal­war kameez did. Ultimately, Varma said, clothes have no re­li­gion and we are who we are.

quiz.q: Which three ideas, often confused, did Amit Varma separate at the start?
quiz.a: The na­tional in­ter­est, pa­tri­o­tism and na­tion­al­ism, which he calls a toxic ide­ol­ogy.

quiz.q: Whose definition of a nation as an imagined political community anchors the episode?
quiz.a: Benedict Anderson’s, from his book *Imagined Communities*, pos­si­bly Varma’s favourite on the sub­ject.

quiz.q: Which 15th-century war do some historians credit with the birth of English consciousness?
quiz.a: The Wars of the Roses, which swept away many feu­dal over­lords and local loy­al­ties.

quiz.q: What did Mussolini promise Italians would rule them, after the First World War?
quiz.a: The tren­choc­racy: the com­mon peo­ple who had fought in the war.

quiz.q: Which two countries fought the 1969 Soccer War after a series of World Cup qualifiers?
quiz.a: Honduras and El Salvador; Varma re­calls about 100 days and six thou­sand dead.

quiz.q: Where, according to Ajay Shah, should a data centre serving Indian users sit?
quiz.a: In Greenland, where the air is cold and re­new­able en­ergy is plen­ti­ful.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 122. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Rabindranath Tagore (Generalstabens litografiska anstalt, public domain); Benedict Anderson (UCD School of Sociology, CC BY 4.0); Neeraj Chopra (Anass Sedrati, CC BY-SA 4.0); Alexander Pushkin (Orest Kiprensky, public domain); Carl Schmitt (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Benito Mussolini (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); George Orwell (Cassowary Colorizations, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Imagined Communities
shelf.creator: Benedict Anderson
shelf.why: Possibly his favourite book on na­tion­al­ism.

shelf.title: History of European Morals
shelf.creator: W. E. H. Lecky
shelf.why: The source of the ‘ex­pand­ing circle’: through his­tory we ex­tend moral con­sid­er­a­tion from fam­ily to tribe to na­tion and be­yond.

shelf.title: The Expanding Circle
shelf.creator: Peter Singer
shelf.why: Singer’s ar­gu­ment that our moral cir­cle keeps widen­ing and will one day in­clude an­i­mals.

shelf.title: The Ferment of Our Founders (Episode 272, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
shelf.why: Shruti Kapila on the fer­ment of India’s founders, the source of her line that Hindutva is ‘a the­ory of vi­o­lence in search of a history’.

shelf.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries
shelf.creator: Manu Pillai
shelf.why: Manu Pillai shows how fluid Hinduism was for cen­turies and how a shared Hindu iden­tity formed grad­u­ally, first against Islam and then against the British and their mis­sion­ar­ies.

shelf.title: The Mahatma and the Poet
shelf.creator: Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore
shelf.why: The Gandhi-Tagore de­bate laid out in full, two great minds dis­agree­ing well: Tagore more rea­soned and right about the dan­gers of na­tion­al­ism, yet see­ing some­thing spe­cial in Gandhi’s force of will.

shelf.title: Essays on Nationalism
shelf.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
shelf.why: A slim, beau­ti­ful book of deep and time­less ideas: Tagore sup­ported Indian in­de­pen­dence yet saw na­tion­al­ism as toxic who­ever wielded it.

shelf.title: The End of History?
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: Fukuyama’s essay cap­tures the post-1989 be­lief that lib­eral democ­racy had won the ar­gu­ment for good.

shelf.title: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
shelf.creator: Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: Mukul’s mas­ter­piece shows how deeply Hindu na­tion­al­ist ideas ran through Indian so­ci­ety over the decades: the com­mu­nal strain was there all along, sec­u­lar lib­er­als were the fringe, and pol­i­tics sim­ply caught up with so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
shelf.why: The con­ver­sa­tional com­pan­ion to Akshaya Mukul’s book on how the Gita Press, through cul­ture and re­li­gion, fed mod­ern po­lit­i­cal Hinduism.

shelf.title: The Sporting Spirit
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: The ‘great essay’ that called sport ‘war minus the shooting’, draw­ing on an ugly foot­ball match in­volv­ing a Moscow team and a riot in Spain.

shelf.title: Vaishnav Vyas’s football Substack
shelf.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
shelf.why: Amit and Vaishnav bond over the thinkers of the game (like Guardiola turn­ing ‘anti-Guardiola’).

shelf.title: The Life and Music of Shubha Mudgal (Episode 426, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shubha Mudgal
shelf.why: ‘My great episode with her’, in which Mudgal re­veals re­vi­sion­ist his­tory and at­tempts to re­name ragas in Hindustani clas­si­cal music.

shelf.title: The Peter Cat Recording Company
shelf.why: The band has a cult fol­low­ing that forms its own com­mu­nity.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on Understanding Labels
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite episodes: what la­bels like lib­eral and con­ser­va­tive re­ally mean, why na­tion­al­ism dif­fers from pa­tri­o­tism, and the hosts’ own con­ser­vatism of chang­ing the world care­fully, one step at a time, be­cause of un­in­tended con­se­quences.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on Fallacies
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode ‘Everything Is Indian, Nothing Is Indian’
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of the show’s most pop­u­lar episodes: al­most ev­ery­thing we con­sider quintessen­tially Indian, from food to clothes to lan­guages, came from else­where and blended to­gether, so get­ting na­tion­al­is­tic about it is ridicu­lous.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything two-parter on globalization and tariffs
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

laughs.text: Amit dates English con­scious­ness to the Wars of the Roses, then dead­pans that The War of the Roses ‘of course, was a 1989 film re­cently made into a film called The Roses, but that is com­pletely dif­fer­ent. Popular cul­ture lovers may not know that it is a tongue in cheek ref­er­ence to some­thing else that hap­pened.’

On Shudh Hindi sound­ing like no­body: imag­ine English speak­ers using only Latinate words, so that in­stead of ‘we shall fight them in the streets’, Winston Churchill had said ‘we shall com­bat them in the boulevards’.

Amit imag­ines Tagore with mod­ern tech: ‘he could have done a YouTube show. Called, and I think he would have called it Everything is Everything. Shob kichu shob kichu.’ He also tells Ajay that what­ever he says against Bengali econ­o­mists, ‘among Bengali philoso­phers, Robi-da stands alone.’
After say­ing it’s ‘not the ideas of Tagore but those of Putin which will thrive’, Amit adds: ‘I never thought I’ll have those two names in the same sen­tence.’

Ajay’s fix for na­tion­al­ism in sport: ‘form teams based on purely ran­dom imag­ined com­mu­ni­ties, put a lit­tle bit of old fash­ioned cap­i­tal­ism into it, have buy­ing and sell­ing of play­ers. And you’re done.’ Amit: in the­ory every Manchester United player could be play­ing for Liverpool five years later, ‘though it is ac­tu­ally prac­ti­cally im­pos­si­ble be­cause none of them would get into that side.’

On biryani being treated as anti-national (the ‘Ajmal Kasab was given biryani’ rhetoric): ‘Biryani is not anti na­tional. You’re right, it is some­what un­healthy, but it is deeply, deeply tasty, es­pe­cially when made well. I am never going to give up biryani.’
Amit on America’s turn to eco­nomic na­tion­al­ism: ‘Like we’re in a bad video game sim­u­la­tion and there’s a bug in the sys­tem and some­thing weird just hap­pened.’
Doug Stanhope on na­tion­al­ism: ‘hat­ing peo­ple you have never met and tak­ing pride in ac­com­plish­ments you had noth­ing to do with’.
Walt Whitman’s ‘we con­tain multitudes’, which Amit ex­tends: ‘Individuals con­tain mul­ti­tudes and mul­ti­tudes of in­di­vid­u­als con­tain fur­ther mul­ti­tudes.’
Ajay: ‘What you want is the press con­fer­ences of Gukesh and Ding’. The gra­cious world chess cham­pi­onship ri­vals are the model of sport­ing con­duct.
Ajay re­calls, at­tribut­ing it to Tagore, the wish for ‘the winds from the seven con­ti­nents to blow through my nation’.
